newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil party bosses discuss civil service reform.
newsitem.headline: Brazil party bosses discuss civil service reform.

text.p: Leaders of government-allied political parties in Brazil met to discuss the chances of putting a controversial civil service reform bill to a first vote in Congress later Wednesday, officials said.

Members of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party (PSDB) were reported to be furious at a proposed compromise which would exempt some categories of public sector workers, including lawmakers, from a ceiling on pay.
"If they approve that in the Chamber (of Deputies), then we'll defeat it in the Senate," senator Jose Serra, one of the PSDB's most senior members, was quoted as saying by several newspapers.

The government has twice been forced to call off a first of two votes in the lower house on the civil service reform bill, principally because of opposition from lawmakers who stand to lose out under the proposed pay ceiling.
An estimated 140 members of the 513-member Chamber of Deputies earn pensions from previous posts in the civil service on top of their 8,000-real ($7,547) monthly salaries.
The ceiling would limit public sector workers to 10,800 reais ($10,188) a month in pay and pensions and is a central element of the reform.

A proposed solution to the impasse put forward Tuesday would allow lawmakers, ministers and the personal aides of senior civil servants to hold onto one pension, even if it took them over the ceiling.

Government economists have said exemptions for some categories of workers would not have a big impact on the overall impact of the reform, which would also allow for the dismissal of currently unfireable employees.

A statement from the Planning Ministry said the reform would allow the federal government, states and municipalities to cut immediately about $6.0 billion from their total $100 billion annual spending on pay.
That saving would rise to about $13.0 billion annually within five years, the statement said.

But the proposed exemptions caused indignation from across the political spectrum and in the media, which has long criticized Congress for refusing to practice the austerity it preaches to the rest of the country.
"Without a doubt, it would increase public scorn for Congress and for the political elite as a whole," wrote columnist Tereza Cruvinel in Wednesday's edition of O Globo.
